newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines awaits key Supreme Court ruling.
newsitem.headline: Philippines awaits key Supreme Court ruling.

text.p: The question of who leads the Philippines into the next century could hang on a ruling this week by the country's Supreme Court.

When the 15-member court meets on Tuesday, the biggest issue it will face is whether to uphold or reverse a previous verdict rejecting moves to amend the constitution and allow President Fidel Ramos to run for a second term in 1998.
Framed in 1987 after Filipinos ousted the widely reviled Ferdinand Marcos from 20 years in power, the charter limits a president to only one term of six years.
The issue has divided business, spurred moves by a fractious political opposition to unite and provoked warnings of instability from the country's influential Roman Catholic Church.
"There is no sense in tempting the fates," said Guillermo Luz, executive director of the elite Makati Business Club.
Credited with turning the economy around with his reform programme, Ramos has repeatedly denied he intends to run for re-election in the May 1997 polls.
The former defence chief and ex-army general said he would be the last person to destroy a constitution he defended by quelling six army coup attempts against his predecessor, Corazon Aquino.
But speculation persists he or his top advisers are behind moves by the citizens group PIRMA -- People's Initiative for Reform, Modernisation and Action -- to amend the constitution.

PIRMA's campaign to collect 15 million signatures to force the calling of a plebiscite that would remove the term limits of incumbent officials collapsed in March when the Supreme Court ruled there was no law allowing such an initiative.
PIRMA has appealed for a reconsideration and court sources said a decision on its appeal would probably be out this week.
Manila newspapers say the court is inclined to sustain the appeal and allow the holding of a referendum.
"This will split the country down the middle," opposition senator and presidential aspirant Edgardo Angara warned.
Luz said business was happy with Ramos but feared the economy would suffer if debates on the constitution diverted attention from reforms still needed to sustain the economic growth.
"The issue is the constitution, not the president," he said.

"I think by and large foreign businessmen would be happy with the prospect of another six years of President Ramos but only on the condition that changing the constitution doesn't herald the return of the days where you changed the rules if you didn't like them," a Western diplomat said.
"As long as it's done democratically, there's nothing intrinsically undemocratic about changing a constitution by popular vote," he added.
A foreign business executive said most business officials were really only concerned about stability and economic opportunities.

"Ramos has shown over the last five years that he is capable of achieving both," he said. "I think the majority of investors would not mind him running again... But if it was through strong-arm tactics then they will be uncomfortable with it."
Political analyst Alex Magno doubted Ramos would run at all. He said the uproar over the constitution was part of a plan to bolster the election chances of the candidate he would endorse.
"At best, it's a tactical move to push for these constitutional reforms," Magno said. "You strengthen Ramos's endorsement -- and you keep the opposition off balance".
